clue.text: "Geography's about maps" — could what history's about be in this pedlar's offering?

definitions.text: "Geography's about maps" — could what history's about be in this pedlar's offering?

parts.words: "Geography's about maps" — could what history's about be in this pedlar's offering?
parts.note: E. C. Bentley's clerihew runs 'Geography is about maps, but Biography is about chaps'; a cheap pamphlet sold by pedlars would then be a book about fellows

explanation.surface: A musing on whether a pedlar's cheap pamphlet could hold the stuff of history, after a famous comic verse.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Bentley's clerihew on biography, whose next line says biography is about 'chaps'; a book of chaps gives the pedlar's ware. A chapman was a travelling pedlar.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheap popular pamphlet of tales or ballads, hawked by itinerant chapmen, is the classic pedlar's offering.

clue.text: The younger was older than the elder at last, and produced the heir at law

definitions.text: The younger was older than the elder at last, and produced the heir at law

parts.words: The younger was older than the elder at last, and produced the heir at law
parts.note: George ... the Younger, son of the elder dramatist, outlived his father and wrote the comedy The Heir at Law

explanation.surface: A family riddle about a son who outlives his father and fathers an heir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the heir at law' looks like a legal heir but is a 1797 comedy by George Colman the Younger; he died older than his father had been.
explanation.definitionFit: Two English dramatists of this surname, father and son, are known as the Elder and the Younger.

clue.text: "We're —- we're the opposite of people!"

parts.note: a line from Tom Stoppard's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead, spoken by the Player about his troupe

explanation.surface: A gap in a theatrical boast that a group is the reverse of ordinary folk.
explanation.walkthrough: The Player in Stoppard's play says his company are the opposite of people: performers rather than audience.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage players are the speaker's troupe, who perform for the people watching.

clue.text: Courage one member got from genie

parts.note: bottle is British slang for nerve or courage
one is I as a Roman numeral
an MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: Someone got pluck from a magic spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: Courage is also a British beer brand, which suits 'bottle'. The definition is the spirit in Stevenson's story The Bottle Imp.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevenson's tale has a demon trapped in a flask who grants wishes, a genie by another name.

clue.text: Former death of Robert Paterson

parts.note: former means old, as in an old flame
mortality means death, as in mortality rates

explanation.surface: The late Robert Paterson's past demise.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Paterson was the Scottish stonemason who tended Covenanters' graves, the title figure of Walter Scott's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott gave the nickname of his gravestone-restorer to his 1816 novel, and Paterson was its real-life original.

clue.text: "His stick, which was a —— lawyer, weighted with lead" (Doyle)

definitions.text: "His stick, which was a —— lawyer, weighted with lead" (Doyle)

parts.words: "His stick, which was a —— lawyer, weighted with lead" (Doyle)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Conan Doyle's The Hound of the Baskervilles; the missing word, with 'lawyer', names a kind of heavy walking stick

explanation.surface: A gap in a Conan Doyle sentence describing a weighted walking stick.
explanation.walkthrough: A Penang lawyer is a walking stick made from a palm stem from the Malaysian island; Doyle's Sir Henry and Stapleton episodes mention one. Fill the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: The island name completes the term for a knobbed palm-wood cudgel, the stick in the quoted line.

clue.text: Principle of Moore — first ever to have illicit connotation

annotationWithheld.why: Principle of Moore — first ever to have illicit connotation (5): ETHIC defined by 'Principle' (Moore's Principia Ethica), but no parse of 'first ever to have illicit connotation' gives the letters
annotationWithheld.clue: Principle of Moore — first ever to have illicit connotation

clue.text: A Wells character attached. The devil you say!

parts.note: Mr Polly is the hero of H. G. Wells's The History of Mr Polly
on means attached, as with a lid on

explanation.surface: A character from H. G. Wells is joined on, provoking an exclamation of surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The devil you say!' reads as an exclamation, but the devil is the fiend Christian fights in Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress.
explanation.definitionFit: The destroying angel of Revelation, the name is given to Satan's champion in Bunyan's allegory.

clue.text: Mean, edgy kind of Trojan prince

indicators.note: kind of suggests a loose version of the two words, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A nervy, stingy young royal from Troy.
explanation.definitionFit: Zeus carried off the beautiful son of King Tros of Troy to be cupbearer of the gods.

clue.text: Scope for questionable historicity given to author of Longitude?

definitions.meaning: scope means freedom or room to act

definitions.text: for questionable historicity given to author of Longitude?
definitions.meaning: the leeway a popular historian such as Dava Sobel, who wrote Longitude, might be allowed with the facts, punning on the companion geographical term

explanation.surface: A complaint that the writer of a popular history book has been allowed too much freedom with the facts.
explanation.definitionFit: Room for manoeuvre is called by the same word as the angular distance from the equator, the partner of longitude.

clue.text: Cast for first Hamlet rehearsal in town

indicators.note: in says the picked letters are placed within the word town
first applies to Hamlet and rehearsal, asking for the opening letter of each word

explanation.surface: A theatre company casts the lead for the first local rehearsal of Hamlet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' takes H and R, which 'in' puts inside TOWN after its T. 'Cast' looks like a theatre noun but is the past participle of throw.
explanation.definitionFit: To cast a stone is to hurl it, so 'cast' as a past participle equals hurled.

clue.text: Do they look after Masefield's work?

definitions.text: Do they look after Masefield's work?

parts.words: Do they look after Masefield's work?
parts.note: Masefield's best-known poem is Cargoes; officers who oversee a ship's freight could be said to supervise it

explanation.surface: A question about who cares for a poet's writings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Masefield's work' is his poem Cargoes, not his oeuvre; the officers in charge of a merchant ship's goods oversee cargoes.
explanation.definitionFit: Officers on merchant ships managing the commercial freight and its sale look after the shipment.

clue.text: Fast morning book

parts.note: Howard Fast wrote a novel of the American Revolution called ... Morning; the clue asks for the first word of its title

explanation.surface: A book to read on a morning when one is fasting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' is the American novelist Howard Fast, not abstinence; his book April Morning supplies the month.
explanation.definitionFit: The month opens the title of Howard Fast's novel about Lexington, so it is the 'morning book' of Fast.

clue.text: Minor work breaks US locum up

indicators.note: breaks tells us the letters of the following words are smashed and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A small piece of writing interrupts an American stand-in doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaks' shuffles US, LOCUM and UP; 'up' looks like a particle with breaks but is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for a little opus, it denotes a short or minor literary or musical composition.

clue.text: Schoolteacher at the crossing from Windsor?

parts.note: a female schoolteacher is a mistress, as in 'maths mistress'
a ford is a shallow place for crossing a river

explanation.surface: A teacher stands at a river crossing near Windsor.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a character in Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor, one of the wives who outwit Falstaff.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Ford is one of the merry wives in Shakespeare's comedy set in Windsor, so she is a lady from that town.

clue.text: Examiner from Irvine quartet

definitions.meaning: an examiner is one who scrutinises closely
The third book of Ian Irvine's fantasy quartet The Well of Echoes

explanation.surface: A tester drawn from a Scottish group of four musicians.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word means one who scrutinises, an inspector or searcher, and titles an Ian Irvine fantasy novel.

clue.text: Saints reported at the head of the column

definitions.text: Saints reported at the head of the column

parts.words: Saints reported at the head of the column
parts.note: early Christian ascetics lived on top of pillars, and a newspaper's column head is where a byline is reported

explanation.surface: A newspaper column headed by news of holy people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'column' suggests journalism, but these holy men, such as Simeon, lived atop stone pillars.
explanation.definitionFit: The pillar-saints of Syria, from Greek stylos for pillar, spent years living on top of columns.

clue.text: Reference by Thomas to H. H. Brackenridge?

definitions.text: Reference by Thomas to H. H. Brackenridge?

parts.words: Reference by Thomas to H. H. Brackenridge?
parts.note: split the American writer's surname into bracken and ridge, a plant and a raised strip of land; Dylan Thomas named a poem after a farm that pairs synonyms of these

explanation.surface: A Welsh poet supposedly alludes to the American writer Hugh Henry Brackenridge.
explanation.walkthrough: Bracken is a kind of fern and a ridge is a hill, so the surname translates into the title of Dylan Thomas's poem about his aunt's farm.
explanation.definitionFit: Dylan Thomas's 1945 poem is named after a Carmarthenshire farm, and its title pairs a plant and a rise in the land.

clue.text: A Shavian upset (3, , 4)

parts.note: the idiom 'upset the ___ ___' with its middle word missing from the count; Bernard Shaw used the phrase for a political comedy

explanation.surface: A Shaw play upsets things, with a teasing word count leaving a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'to upset the apple cart' means to spoil plans; Shaw's 1928 play takes its title from it. The blank in the count stands for the omitted middle word.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's political extravaganza is titled after the cart one upsets in the idiom for ruining arrangements.

clue.text: American novelist — also producing verse now and then

definitions.text: American novelist — also producing verse now and then

parts.words: American novelist — also producing verse now and then
parts.note: Robert Penn ... wrote All the King's Men and was also a poet laureate of the United States

explanation.surface: A US writer of fiction who occasionally turns out poems.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Penn Warren, author of All the King's Men, won Pulitzers for both fiction and poetry.

clue.text: Place for all visitors said to be suggested instead

definitions.text: Place for all visitors said to be suggested instead

parts.words: Place for all visitors said to be suggested instead
parts.note: the ship's call 'all ... that's going ...' tells visitors to leave the vessel for land

explanation.surface: A host proposes a different spot for every guest.
explanation.walkthrough: Before a liner sails, visitors are told to go to land; the place for them is off the ship.
explanation.definitionFit: On land, off the ship, is where visitors to a departing vessel are directed to go.

clue.text: His work was all done from memory

definitions.text: His work was all done from memory

parts.words: His work was all done from memory
parts.note: Joseph ... monitorial schools taught by rote, the pupils reciting their lessons by heart

explanation.surface: Praise for a performer who never needed notes.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Lancaster, the educational reformer, built a system of rote learning in which pupils taught one another by repetition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Quaker reformer's monitorial method relied on drilling and recitation, learning by heart rather than by reasoning.

clue.text: Learn about him in The Flying Dutchman

indicators.note: about signals that the letters of Learn are turned around and reordered

explanation.surface: Study the man who appears in Wagner's opera about the phantom ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Flying Dutchman' suggests Wagner, but it is a 1939 novel by Michael Arlen, the author of The Green Hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Arlen, the Armenian-born British novelist, wrote a book titled The Flying Dutchman, so he is in it as author.

clue.text: This holds a clue to a novel from France

definitions.text: clue to a novel from France
definitions.note: the definition reads as the answer to a clue for a French novel: the title solves it

indicators.note: holds means the word This contains another letter within it

explanation.surface: A text contains a hint pointing towards a French novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds' places A inside THIS. The novel is Anatole France's, so 'from France' names the author as well as the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Anatole France's 1890 novel about an Alexandrian courtesan, later Massenet's opera, carries this title.

clue.text: Some attempts by Knox's interpreter

definitions.meaning: attempts or tests, as in tryouts
Ronald Knox, who made his own translation of the Bible

explanation.surface: A few efforts made by someone translating for Knox.
explanation.definitionFit: Tests or attempts are plural tryouts; the word also opens Knox's title about the hardships of translating.

clue.text: Falsify negative for Fleming's character

parts.note: to doctor accounts is to falsify them
no is the negative answer

explanation.surface: Faking a refusal for one of Ian Fleming's people.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian Fleming's villain Julius No, title figure of the 1958 Bond novel, is a character of his.

clue.text: Strait man from Powys

definitions.meaning: a strait is a narrow channel of sea, here the one between the Isle of Wight and mainland England
Wolf ... is the hero of John Cowper Powys's novel of that name

explanation.surface: A straight-talking man from the Welsh county of Powys.
explanation.walkthrough: Powys looks like the Welsh county but is the novelist John Cowper Powys, author of Wolf Solent.
explanation.definitionFit: The channel separating the Isle of Wight from Hampshire bears the name that is also the surname of Powys's hero.

clue.text: Alienate Sargent? That's out of order, even with English leader

indicators.note: a word's leader is its opening letter, here the start of English
out of order says the letters of Sargent are disordered and rearranged

explanation.surface: Upsetting the painter Sargent by mixing him up, even with an Englishman in front.
explanation.walkthrough: Sargent is the painter, and 'out of order' rearranges his name into a word meaning odd; 'leader' supplies the first letter of English, set in front.
explanation.definitionFit: To estrange someone is to make them hostile or distant, the same as to alienate them.
